1366.title: Lal Ded at the table
1366.hook: a heaped plate, an empty one, and a proud faster: Lal Ded and the Gita on why a Hindu fast is for God, not for the score
1366.carry: in measure, without pride: the gita's middle road
1366.tomorrow: Gargi asks what everything is woven on.
1366.howItsDone: Lal Ded's vakhs, this one among them, are recited and sung in Kashmiri; in many Hindu homes the Gita's brahmarpanam verse is said before meals.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lal Ded's two strips of cloth, knotted for every insult and every bow, weighed the same at evening.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: In plenty of Hindu homes, someone is fasting this week. A Monday fast for Shiva. Ekadashi, the eleventh day of the moon, for Vishnu. Nine nights of Navratri for the Goddess. Fasting runs all through this faith. So here's a fair question: is the person who eats least the most spiritual one at the table? Lal Ded, the Kashmiri poet-saint we've spent four days with, has a short saying that catches the overeater and the proud faster at once, and then points to a door.
screen: `A MONDAY FAST. EKADASHI. NAVRATRI.` → `IS LESS ALWAYS HOLIER?` → `A SAYING THAT CATCHES BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase. Eat and eat, and you'll get nowhere. Stop eating, and you'll grow proud. Eat in measure, and you'll become even, and the bolted doors will open. The first line is easy to hear. The second has the sting. Not eating doesn't make you holy. It can make you proud. Lal Ded wandered as a seeker and knew the hard road. Of all people, she could have praised it. Instead she warns that it has its own trap: being pleased with yourself for how little you need. Then the middle: eat in measure, become even, and the bolted doors swing open. She doesn't say which doors; many readers hear the doors within. The Bhagavad Gita has a neighbor to this saying, in paraphrase: yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. Elsewhere it says it plainly: evenness is called yoga. Here's the teaching under both. In Hinduism a fast, a vrat, is a vow offered to God, not a contest. And the ego, ahamkara, the voice that says look what I did, can feed on anything, even on going without. That's why Lal Ded aims at the pride, not the hunger.
screen: `TOO MUCH GETS YOU NOWHERE` · `TOO LITTLE MAKES YOU PROUD` · `EVENNESS IS CALLED YOGA` · `A VRAT IS FOR GOD, NOT THE SCORE`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, or now with a glass of water, pause before the first bite or sip. Many Hindu families say a verse from the Gita here, brahmarpanam, offering the food to God before eating it, so the meal is about who it's for, not more or less. Look at what's in front of you: not heaped, not empty, enough. If you pray, offer it silently; if you don't, take one slow bite and notice that it's enough.
Lal Ded. The poet who said eating too much gets you nowhere, not eating makes you proud, and eating in measure opens the bolted doors. Today's word.
screen: `LAL DED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in measure, without pride, the Gita's middle road. Not heaped, not empty. Rest well.

1367.title: Gargi's questions
1367.word: in their own words where they exist
1367.hook: warned 'don't ask too much, or your head will fall off', Gargi comes back with two questions, and the answer is Brahman
1367.carry: everything is woven on brahman, the imperishable
1367.tomorrow: Maitreyi asks what wealth can't buy.
1367.howItsDone: Gargi's questions are read and studied wherever the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is taught.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Lal Ded: too much gets you nowhere, too little makes you proud, and in measure the doors open.
screen: `LAL DED.`

segments.voice: Don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. That's a line from an Upanishad, said in a king's hall in front of learned men, to a woman who wouldn't stop asking questions. Her name is Gargi, and you first met her back in year two. She falls silent. And later, in the same debate, she stands up again. Akka and Lalla left sayings of their own. Other women's words didn't survive at all. And some, like Gargi's, speak inside a text that's mostly about someone else. Where their words exist, we listen.
screen: `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH.` → `A WOMAN WHO KEEPS ASKING.` → `HER WORDS INSIDE ANOTHER STORY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. King Janaka of Videha has called the wise to his court, and the sage Yajnavalkya is answering all comers. Gargi steps forward. Her question, in paraphrase: all this world is woven back and forth on water, like threads on a loom. So on what is water woven? On wind, he says. And wind? On the sky. Layer after layer, each answer becomes her next question. Then Yajnavalkya stops her: Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. And she falls silent. It's easy to stop there, as if she lost. The text doesn't. Later she rises again and tells the assembly: I will ask him two questions. The Upanishad pictures her like a warrior stringing a bow and taking up two arrows. That which is above the sky and below the earth, and between them, past, present and future: on what is it woven? In space, he answers. And space, on what is that woven? This time he names what's under everything: the imperishable, which the wise call Brahman. It sees and is not seen, hears and is not heard. Gargi tells the assembly none of them will beat him. That's one of the great teachings of the Upanishads: under every layer of the world is one reality, Brahman, and everything is woven on it. And notice how it arrived. Not as a decree. As the answer to a woman's questions. The Upanishads teach by asking.
screen: `A DEBATE IN KING JANAKA'S HALL` · `ON WHAT IS IT WOVEN?` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH` · `TWO ARROWS: THE IMPERISHABLE, BRAHMAN`

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, a cup, a hand, the floor, and ask quietly, the way the Upanishads ask: on what is this woven? What holds it up? Let an answer come, then ask the same of that answer. When you reach the place where no answer comes, don't push; rest there in the question, the way Gargi did when she fell silent. If you pray, rest there before God.
In their own words, where they exist: Gargi, warned not to ask too much, who came back with two questions like arrows. Today's word.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: everything is woven on Brahman, the imperishable. A warning didn't end her questions. See you tomorrow.

1368.title: Maitreyi's question
1368.word: in their own words where they exist
1368.hook: offered a share of the property, Maitreyi asks what wealth can't give, and Yajnavalkya teaches the Self, the atman
1368.carry: all is dear for the sake of the self
1368.tomorrow: a saint who signed her hymns as a ghoul.
1368.howItsDone: The dialogue of Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi is read and taught as part of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi, warned not to ask too much, came back with two questions, and the answer: everything is woven on Brahman, the imperishable.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: A man is about to leave home for good, to live as a wandering seeker. Before he goes, he does the responsible thing: he sits down with his wife to settle the property, so that she and his other wife will be provided for. The will, the house, the money. His wife listens. Then, instead of asking how much, she asks something else entirely. The man is Yajnavalkya again, the sage Gargi questioned. The wife is Maitreyi, whom you first met in year one.
screen: `A MAN ABOUT TO LEAVE HOME.` → `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY.` → `MAITREYI ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi he's about to leave this life at home, and wants to make a settlement between her and Katyayani, his other wife. Maitreyi answers, in paraphrase: sir, if this whole earth, filled with wealth, were mine, would I become immortal by it? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich; there's no hope of immortality through wealth. Then her line: what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. She isn't refusing to be provided for. She's refusing to let the property be the whole conversation. The text has him say she is dear to him, and speaks dear words. Then he teaches. A husband is dear, he says, not for the husband's own sake, but for the sake of the Self. A wife, children, wealth, the world itself: all dear for the sake of the Self. It's the Self that must be seen, heard, thought on, and meditated upon. That Self is the atman, the deepest you, and the same Upanishad says in a famous line: this Self is Brahman. Here's the teaching. Hindus name four aims of life: dharma, what's right; artha, wealth; kama, pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Wealth is a real aim, not a sin. Maitreyi doesn't scorn it. She simply knows which aim it can't reach.
screen: `THE TALK ABOUT THE PROPERTY` · `WOULD WEALTH MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` · `DEAR FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF` · `DHARMA · ARTHA · KAMA · MOKSHA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're working toward or wanting right now, a purchase, a grade, a result, and hold it gently. Hindu teachers call this kind of sorting viveka, discernment. Ask Maitreyi's question of it, without judging: what would I do with this? What can it give, and what can't it? Then turn toward whatever feels deeper than the thing itself and rest there; if you pray, bring that deeper want before God.
In their own words, where they exist. Today, Maitreyi, offered a share of the property, asking what she would do with what can't make her immortal. Today's word.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all is dear for the sake of the Self. One question, asked at the edge of a goodbye. That's today.

1369.title: The ghoul of Karaikkal
1369.word: in their own words where they exist
1369.hook: a poet signs her hymns as a ghoul of the cremation ground, where Shiva dances: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, and why Shaivas wear sacred ash

1369.howItsDone: Tamil Shaivas honor Karaikkal Ammaiyar among the Nayanars; her hymns are sung as part of the Tirumurai, her image is found in Shiva temples near the dancing Shiva, and devotees wear vibhuti, sacred ash, on the forehead.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreyi asked for what wealth can't give, and heard: all is dear for the sake of the Self.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: At the end of a hymn, the poet signs her name. This poet doesn't sign as a saint, or a lady, or a devotee. She signs as a pey, a ghoul, the kind of gaunt spirit said to haunt the burning grounds. The pey of Karaikkal. Earlier on this path we met her at her own door, giving away a mango. Today, the name she gave herself.
screen: `A POET SIGNS HER NAME.` → `NOT A SAINT: A GHOUL.` → `THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL.`

segments.voice: Her story is in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints. Her name was Punitavati, a merchant's wife in Karaikkal. After the mango, her husband grew afraid of her and left. So she asked Shiva to take away the beauty she had kept for him, and give her the body of a pey instead, bones and sinew, fit only for praising him. The story says she climbed Shiva's mountain upside down, so her feet wouldn't touch its holy ground, and that Shiva, seeing her, called her Mother. So she's known as Karaikkal Ammaiyar, the mother of Karaikkal. Now her own words, in paraphrase. Her hymns picture Shiva dancing at night in the cremation ground, among flames, ash and owls, with ghouls dancing around him. Among them is the singer herself, signing as the pey of Karaikkal. She didn't hide the bones; she signed with them. In Shaiva tradition Shiva is the Lord of the burning ground, the one who is there when everything else has gone to ash. Many Shaiva teachers give the same meaning to vibhuti, the sacred ash devotees wear in three lines on the forehead: everything ends in ash, and Shiva remains. Shiva himself is pictured smeared in ash. She took that to its edge, and stopped dressing up for anyone. And today? When looks, titles and what people call you start to feel like everything, the ash on a Shaiva forehead says: those burn. What you give to Shiva remains. Her hymns are kept in the Tirumurai, the sacred Shaiva collection, and with her, this season of women closes.
screen: `PUNITAVATI ASKS FOR A NEW BODY` · `SHIVA CALLS HER MOTHER` · `SHE SIGNS AS THE PEY OF KARAIKKAL` · `VIBHUTI: ALL BURNS, SHIVA REMAINS`

segments.voice: If your family keeps vibhuti, take a small pinch; if not, just touch your thumb to your forehead. Many Shaivas draw the ash in three lines, some saying namah shivaya as they do. Think, gently: this body will end in ash. Not as a scare; as a relief. Let the names people call you, the roles, the looks, settle like ash, one at a time. If you pray, offer what's left to Shiva; if you don't, sit with what remains when those are gone.
In their own words, where they exist: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, called Mother in the story, who signed her hymns as the pey of Karaikkal. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: sacred ash, all burns, Shiva remains. Mother in the story, pey in her own hand. A season closes here.

segments.voice: A sealed door in the great temple at Chidambaram, the temple of Shiva as the dancer. Behind it, tradition says, lies a room long left unopened. Outside stands a Chola king. He has heard a few verses of the old Tamil hymns to Shiva sung at his court, and he wants the rest. The priests won't open the door. Only the singers who made these hymns, they say, can open it, and those singers are long gone. A new part of the path begins here: the regional traditions, starting in the Tamil south.
screen: `A SEALED DOOR AT CHIDAMBARAM.` → `A KING WHO WANTS THE HYMNS.` → `ONLY THE SINGERS CAN OPEN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, as tradition tells it, in paraphrase. If only the saints can open the door, the king will bring the saints. He has images of the three singers, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, carried through the streets in procession and set before the room. The door opens. Inside are the palm leaves the hymns were written on, much of them eaten away by white ants. Then, the story says, a voice is heard: what this age needs has been kept. A learned devotee, Nambi Andar Nambi, gathers what survives and sets it in order, and the hymns are sung again. That gathering is the Tevaram, at the heart of the Tirumurai, the Tamil Shaiva canon. The story doesn't pretend nothing was lost; the ants got there first. And look at the hymns themselves. They're in Tamil, not Sanskrit, and they're tied to places. A hymn praises the Shiva of this town, by this river, in this grove. The singers walked from shrine to shrine, and the temples they sang are still known as the places that were sung. Here's the teaching. Hindus believe the one God, present everywhere, also truly dwells in a particular temple, in a particular form, and can be praised in your own mother tongue. That's why temple singers, oduvars, still sing these Tamil hymns in worship. And in the story, the key to the room was the singers themselves.
screen: `THE SAINTS CARRIED TO THE DOOR` · `PALM LEAVES EATEN BY ANTS` · `WHAT THIS AGE NEEDS WAS KEPT` · `THE SHIVA OF THIS PLACE, IN TAMIL`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one temple, shrine or home altar you know: its smell, its light, the sound of it. If you don't pray, picture the place and what it holds for the people who go there, and give thanks for what was kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday began the Tevaram, Shiva praised in Tamil, place by place: a sealed room, and palm leaves eaten by ants.
screen: `THE TEVARAM: SHIVA PRAISED IN TAMIL, PLACE BY PLACE.`

segments.voice: The wedding is under way. The groom is a handsome young man named Arurar, the families are gathered, the rites have begun. Then an old Brahmin pushes through the crowd, holding up a palm-leaf deed. This young man, he announces, is my slave. His grandfather signed him over to me, him and all his line. The groom loses his temper, calls the old man a madman, and tears the deed to pieces. That insult, the story says, is how one of the Tevaram's three singers found his first word.
screen: `A WEDDING UNDER WAY.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH A DEED.` → `YOU MADMAN.`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam tells it, in paraphrase. The old man isn't put off. That was only a copy, he says; the original is kept in his own town. So the wedding party follows him there, and before the village elders he produces the deed. They compare the handwriting with the grandfather's. It matches. The groom is bound. Then the old man leads them toward the temple, walks inside, and vanishes. It was Shiva. And Shiva speaks to the young man: you called me a madman, so sing of me, and begin with that word. The young man, known ever after as Sundarar, opens his first hymn with it. In paraphrase: madman, wearing the crescent moon in your hair. The name he shouted in anger becomes praise. Here's the teaching. In Tamil Shaivism, grace, arul, comes first: Shiva goes looking for his devotee before the devotee goes looking for him. He didn't wait for good manners; he took the insult and handed it back as a first line. And bhakti lets you stand before God in more than one way. Devotees are called adiyar, the Lord's servants, and Sundarar's calling begins with a deed saying exactly that. Yet the tradition gives him a second title too, the Lord's friend. Servant and friend, in one man, free to talk back. The wedding didn't happen; that's a hard ending for a bride, and the story doesn't hide it.
screen: `THE DEED IS REAL` · `THE OLD MAN WAS SHIVA` · `GRACE COMES FIRST: ARUL` · `SERVANT AND FRIEND`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you said recently in frustration, a sharp word aimed at a person, at life, or at God, and without scolding yourself, hear it again quietly. Ask what longing is hidden inside it. Then say it again, plainly, the way Tamil bhakti allows: to God, as a friend who can take it. If you pray, let it become the first line of a prayer, the way Sundarar's did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sundarar began his first hymn with the word he shouted: madman. Shiva claims his servant, and calls him friend. A week from Lal Ded in Kashmir to the Tamil south.
screen: `TAMIL SHAIVISM AND THE TEVARAM.`

segments.voice: A messenger arrives with an order from the king: come to court. The man being summoned is a singer of Shiva, carrying a small hoe, the kind used to pull grass from between the stones of a temple courtyard. The stories call him Appar. Then, instead of packing a bag, he answers with a song. Its opening, in paraphrase: we are subjects of no one, and we do not fear death. The messenger goes back carrying a hymn instead of a prisoner.
screen: `AN ORDER FROM THE KING.` → `AN OLD MAN WITH A HOE.` → `A SONG SENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Appar's life is told in the Periya Puranam, the book of the lives of the Shaiva saints. It says he spent a long time on another path and then came home to Shiva, and that the king was angry about it. So the order is a threat, not an invitation. The song, in paraphrase: we are no one's subjects, we do not fear death, we will not suffer in hell, we do not tremble, we know no sickness, we bow to no one, because we belong to the Lord. This isn't a protest against kings in general. It's a statement about belonging. If his whole life is Shiva's, there's no room left for a second master. Then look at the hoe. The man who bows to no king spends his days on his knees, pulling weeds from temple stones so others can walk there barefoot. Tradition says the king had him tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the sea, and that Appar sang the five syllables, namah shivaya, and the stone floated him to shore. Some take that as a plain miracle; others hear a picture of what the name of Shiva can hold up. Here's the teaching. Those five syllables, the panchakshara, are the heart mantra of Shaivas, said at home, in temples, on prayer beads, every day. Namah shivaya means bowing to Shiva. Say it, and you've said whom you belong to. Which voice do you finally answer to?
screen: `A SUMMONS THAT IS A THREAT` · `SUBJECTS OF NO ONE` · `THE STONE THAT FLOATED` · `NAMAH SHIVAYA: WHOM YOU BELONG TO`

segments.voice: Notice the voices that summon you today, a message, a deadline, somebody's opinion, and name them one at a time without pushing them away. Then ask quietly: under all of these, what do I answer to in the end? Let the answer be a word, a person, a promise, or God, and if you pray, say the five syllables Appar sang, namah shivaya, slowly with the breath.
